newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Filipino vigilantes emerge from shadows with arms.
newsitem.headline: Filipino vigilantes emerge from shadows with arms.

text.p: A shadowy group of Christian vigilantes came out into the open for the first time on Saturday and showed high-powered weapons they said they would use to fight a peace deal between Manila and Moslem rebels.

"If the government rams the (deal) down their throats, they will be forced to fight back," city councillor Jaime Cabato told reporters in a clandestine meeting between the group and media which he had helped arrange.

The meeting took place outside Zamboanga city, a bastion of Christian opposition to the peace deal which formally ended a 24-year revolt for Moslem self-rule waged by the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) in the southern Mindanao region.
The deal calls for the establishment of an MNLF-led administrative council to supervise development in 14 Mindanao provinces and nine cities, including Zamboanga.
Up until now, the vigilante group, called Mindanao Christian Unified Command (MCUC), had been a name in newspapers only.

It took its first action against the peace accord when it exploded five home-made bombs in nearby Dumingag town a few days before the agreement was signed in Manila on Monday in the presence of President Fidel Ramos and Islamic diplomats.
About 35 vigilantes appeared at the meeting with Filipino and foreign journalists and showed them weapons ranging from Armalite assault rifles to machineguns and grenade launchers.
Clad in fatigues bearing insignias of an inverted Philippine flag to signify they were at war, they conducted drills while wearing ski masks to hide their identities.
"Viva (Long live) Zamboanga, Viva Mindanao," they shouted as they marched in a clearing in a banana plantation about 20 km (12 miles) from central Zamboanga city.
Commanders of the group said the vigilantes would serve as defence forces in their respective villages to prevent intrusions by MNLF men into their communities.
Although the country's five million Moslem minority regard the area as their ancestral homeland, they are outnumbered 3-to-1 in the area by Christian settlers.
Christians have accused Manila of a sell-out for signing the accord. Many have expressed fears that Moslems might take their lands back if the MNLF gains political ascendancy in the region.
"Once they do that, that's when we will react," said one vigilante leader who refused to be identified.
Philippine officials in Manila have said Christian fears that Moslems would take possession of their lands were baseless.
Cabato said the men were part of a larger group numbering 3,000 vigilantes scattered in different areas and including former soldiers.
The military played down reports of the existence of Christian vigilantes.
"I have not seen this group, although we are trying to monitor them," Zamboanga defence command chief Warlito Sayam told reporters.
